new_groups.label: Bishop Moore's letter to the Evening Post, 12 July 1804, on General Hamilton's last hours
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter from Bishop Moore, dated Thursday evening, 12 July 1804, to Mr. Coleman of the New York Evening Post: 'The public mind being extremely agitated by the melancholy fate of that great man, Alexander Hamilton, I have thought it would be grateful to my fellow citizens, would provide against misrepresentation, and, perhaps, be conducive to the advancement of the cause of religion, were I to give a narrative of some facts which have fallen under my own observation, during the time which elapsed between the fatal duel and his departure out of this world.' The bishop's own account of his visits and of the communion he gave.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Gouverneur Morris's oration at General Hamilton's funeral: 'If on this sad, this solemn occasion'
new_groups.definition: Printings of the oration Gouverneur Morris delivered at General Hamilton's funeral in New York, as the Evening Post gave it, saying that those who heard it 'all agree that it comes near enough to what was actually delivered, to be presented as the oration at length': 'Fellow-citizens, If on this sad, this solemn occasion, I should endeavour to move your commiseration, it would be doing injustice to that sensibility which has been so generally and so justly manifested.' The speaker's words as reported; two papers name him 'Governor Morris'.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The correspondence between General Hamilton and Colonel Burr, published at New York, July 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of the publication that began in the New York Evening Post of 16 July 1804: an address 'TO THE AMERICAN PUBLIC' ('The shocking catastrophe which has recently occurred, terminating the life of Alexander Hamilton, and which has spread a gloom over our city that will not be speedily dissipated, demands that the circumstances which led to it, or were intimately connected with it, should not be concealed from the world'), then 'the correspondence that passed between General Hamilton and Colonel Burr', the letters numbered from No. 1 (Burr's letter of 18 June 1804: 'I send for your perusal a letter signed Charles D. Cooper'), with the statement agreed by the two seconds. Most papers printed it over one or two issues; the National Intelligencer and the New Hampshire Gazette begin with the correspondence itself. The two men's own letters, and the seconds' account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Hamilton's will, signed 9 July 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of Alexander Hamilton's will: 'In the name of God, Amen. I, Alexander Hamilton, of the city of New-York, Counsellor at Law, do make this my last Will and Testament', which names three executors, is signed on the ninth day of July 1804 and is certified at the New York Surrogate's Office on 16 July. Most papers print it after Hamilton's statement and the Evening Post's note 'On the foregoing letters and papers, the Editor will make no comment'. The document itself; the excerpts end before the executors' names.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: General Hamilton's statement 'On my expected interview with Col. Burr', found with his will
new_groups.definition: Printings of the paper General Hamilton left with his will, numbered No. 12 in the publication (No. 13 in the National Intelligencer, No. XII in Jenks' Portland Gazette): 'On my expected interview with Col. Burr, I think it proper to make some remarks explanatory of my conduct, motives and views', beginning 'My religious and moral principles are strongly opposed to the practice of duelling'. Most papers introduce it as 'inclosed with his will and some other papers in a packet addressed to one of his executors'. Hamilton's own words, written before the meeting.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The coroner's jury on General Hamilton's death, August 1804: a verdict of murder against Aaron Burr, as the papers reported it
new_groups.definition: Printings of the New York reports, dated 3, 4 and 13 August 1804, of the verdict of the jury of inquest that the coroner summoned on General Hamilton's death: most quote it, 'That Aaron Burr, Esq. Vice President of the United States, was guilty of the murder of Alexander Hamilton' (three papers print 'is guilty'), and name the two seconds as accessaries; a shorter New York paragraph says the inquest 'brought in a verdict of MURDER by AARON BURR', and the Norfolk Gazette gives it in its own words. The accounts are counted together, as 1805 counted the accounts of Judge Chase's acquittal and 1807 the Burr verdict; the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer printed two accounts and the Enquirer three. An inquest's verdict, which accuses a named public man; the excerpts end before the seconds' names.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A letter from Wythe Court-House, Virginia, 30 July 1804: 'the Clinch Mountain had sunk'
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from a gentleman at Wythe Court-House, Virginia, to his friend in Frederick-Town, Maryland, dated 30 July 1804: 'We have for 12 days been clouded with a dark smoke, and this day I was informed by a gentleman from Kentucky that the Clinch Mountain had sunk for many miles to the depth of 50 feet'; the writer supposes it 'occasioned by the burning of the stone coal which is in the mountain'. Two papers print a shorter form headed 'Singular Phenomenon', without the date and with 'for ten days'; the Rhode-Island Republican also prints 'ten days', and the Norfolk Gazette 'twelve days' in words. A report at second hand: the writer passes on what a traveller told him.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: An armed party marches against the Spanish fort of Baton Rouge in West Florida, August 1804: two reports from Natchez
new_groups.definition: Two reports from Natchez, in the Mississippi Territory, of an armed party that marched from near the line with Spanish West Florida against the fort of Baton Rouge in August 1804 and posted a paper declaring West Florida free. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Natchez, August 1804: a letter of 7 August on armed men with a flag near Bayou Sara
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter dated 7 August 1804, published at Natchez on 10 August: 'Returning this morning from the vicinity of Little Bayou-Sara, I met not far from the line, 21 armed men;—on passing a house within my view, they sounded a French horn, and unfurled a flag composed of four white and three blue stripes'. Two papers print it under the heading 'Unpleasant Symptoms'. An unsigned letter-writer's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Natchez, 14 August 1804: 'Mr. Nathan Kemper, with a party of about 30 men, with colors flying and horns sounding' marches on Baton Rouge
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Natchez report of 14 August 1804: 'By a gentleman arrived here yesterday from the neighbourhood of Bayou Sarah, we have been favored with the following information. That Mr. Nathan Kemper, with a party of about 30 men, with colors flying and horns sounding, marched from the neighbourhood of the line of demarcation between this Territory and West-Florida, on the 7th inst. against the fort of Baton Rouge' (the wording varies a little between papers); it gives a paper posted at the party's headquarters: 'For a people to be free, it is sufficient that they will it.' A report at second hand from a traveller, with the party's own declaration.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Spanish minister Yrujo and W. Jackson of the Political Register, September and October 1804
new_groups.definition: Two publications in a dispute between the Marquis de Casa Yrujo, the Spanish minister to the United States, and W. Jackson of the Philadelphia Political Register, in September and October 1804: Jackson's statement with a deposition and letters, and the minister's letter to the Secretary of State in reply. Each side's own account. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: W. Jackson's statement in the Political Register, September 1804, with a deposition and letters concerning the Spanish minister
new_groups.definition: Printings of a publication from the Philadelphia Political Register, dated 20 September 1804 in two papers: 'In the discharge of an important, and to myself an indispensable duty, the subjoined statement was communicated, in the first instance, to the government.—In a respectful solicitude for the rights and interest of our country the deposition and letters are now made public. W. Jackson.' The statement, deposition and letters that follow concern the Marquis de Casa Yrujo, the Spanish minister. One side's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Marquis de Casa Yrujo's letter to the Secretary of State, published at his request, October 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter from the Spanish minister to the Secretary of State, published in the National Intelligencer of 5 October 1804 'at the request of the Marquis de Casa Yrujo': 'Having been absent from Philadelphia for these 18 days past and travelled far into a part of Virginia where I had no opportunity to see the late newspapers from the Northward', he answers the publication in the Political Register (the other group). The minister's own account; the New Hampshire Gazette and the Kentucky Gazette misprint his name 'Trujo' (their transcriptions read 'Trujillo'), and the Oracle Post prints the letter over two issues.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Secretary of State's notice that the amendment on electing the President and Vice-President has been ratified, 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of a public notice 'By James Madison, Secretary of State of the United States', given 'in pursuance of the Act of Congress passed on the 26th March last' (the act supplementary to the act relative to the election of a President and Vice-President): 'That the amendment proposed, during the last session of Congress, to the Constitution of the United States, respecting the manner of voting for President and Vice-President of the United States, has been ratified by the Legislatures of three fourths of the several states', which it names. Several papers ran it in successive issues, and each printing counts, as 1807 counted the proclamation calling Congress. The government's notice.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Ursuline nuns of New Orleans to the President, and his answer, 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter to the editor of the Moniteur (the Louisiana Monitor) of New Orleans, dated 12 September 1804: 'The following memorial was addressed by the Ursuline Nuns of this city to the President of the United States', with the memorial ('Emboldened by the favourable mention you have been pleased to make of their Order, the Nuns of Ursula ...') and the President's answer ('I have received, holy Sisters, the letter you have written me, wherein you express anxiety for the property vested in your institution, by the former governments of Louisiana'). Jenks' Portland Gazette prints the memorial and the answer without the letter to the editor. The nuns' and the President's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Commodore Preble's letter off Tripoli, 14 June 1804: Mr. O'Brien sent on shore 'to endeavour to ransom our unfortunate countrymen'
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Commodore Preble to the Secretary of the Navy, dated 14 June 1804, on board the frigate Constitution off Tripoli, published by the government in Washington on 2 November: 'Yesterday I anchored off the harbour, and sent Mr. O'Brien on shore under a flag of truce, to endeavour to ransom our unfortunate countrymen'. The commodore's own report.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A motion in the House, 12 November 1804: Mr. Griswold asks for an inquiry into drawbacks of duties on goods shipped on from New Orleans
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the House of Representatives' proceedings of Monday 12 November 1804, in the National Intelligencer's words: 'Mr. Griswold stated that some inconvenience had been felt by some of the merchants of the Atlantic ports in making shipments to New Orleans, as they were not authorized to obtain drawbacks on a re-shipment from that port to a foreign country', and moved 'That the committee of Commerce and Manufactures be instructed to enquire into the expediency of allowing, under proper regulations, a drawback of duties on goods, wares and merchandise, imported into the port of New Orleans from any port of the United States, and from thence exported to any foreign port or place'; 'The resolution was carried nem. con.' The papers printed it inside their reports of the House's proceedings; it is counted as an item, as 1806 counted Mr. Gregg's resolution and 1800 Mr. Livingston's. A member's motion and the House's vote, as reported.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message to Congress, 8 November 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of the President's annual message delivered to both Houses on 8 November 1804 by his secretary: 'To a people, fellow citizens, who sincerely desire the happiness and prosperity of other nations; to those who justly calculate that their own well being is advanced by that of the nations with which they have intercourse, it will be a satisfaction to observe that the war which was lighted up in Europe a little before our last meeting, has not yet extended its flames to other nations'. It speaks of the irregularities on the ocean, Louisiana and Spain, the Indian tribes, the Barbary powers and the revenue. Policy arguments in the President's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The documents sent to Congress with the President's message, November 1804: Spain's minister of state on the cession of Louisiana
new_groups.definition: Printings of the documents that accompanied a message from the President to Congress in November 1804, published in the National Intelligencer of 14 November as 'DOCUMENT No. I' and onward, counted by the first: an extract of a letter from Don Pedro Cevallos, minister of state of his Catholic Majesty, to Charles Pinckney, dated at the Pardo, 10 February 1804, in translation: 'his majesty has thought fit to renounce his opposition to the alienation of Louisiana made by France'. The documents that follow include the correspondence on the act of Congress that allowed the President to erect the shores and waters of the bay and river of Mobile into a collection district. The Spanish government's and the two governments' ministers' own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1804 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1804 that reach 3 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 1,691 items printed somewhere, 129 in 7 or more papers by the finder's count, 47 in 9 or more). Because the amendment on electing the President, the Louisiana treaty and the acts of the session sit in families that began in 1803, the same script was also run with year 1803 over the 1804 pages (items_from_1803.json: 183 items, 12 in 7 or more). Every item in 7 or more papers was read in this session (Claude, the session's own model; no second reader). Each chosen item and each candidate set aside was counted item by item with phrase searches on all 3,472 pages of 1804 in both transcriptions (story_phrase_search.py, phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json); every hit was read. Four printings stand on pages whose transcriptions are too garbled for the phrases and were found by reading.
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1805, 1807, 1808 and 1809: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests of unrelated paragraphs (a single paragraph of the House's daily proceedings is counted as an item, as 1806, 1809 and 1800 did); items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months from January to December and the main kinds of news. Every story alike (the owner's rule of 11 November 2026): no item was left out for its subject. Stories are counted item by item; where several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story, and where one publication holds several documents, each document is counted by its own words. A sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent reaches 7 (two here: the two reports of the articles against Judge Chase, 6 papers each). A group count is a target, not a quota.

counted_item_by_item.Laws printed by authority: The item finder chains the acts of the first session of the Eighth Congress through their enacting formula and the list of acts (items of 7 to 9 papers and up to 94 printings). Counted by its own text, no act reaches 7 papers: the act erecting Louisiana into two territories, the act for duties on imports and tonnage in the ceded territories, the act supplementary on the election of a President and Vice-President, and the act to protect commerce and seamen against the Barbary powers are in 5 or 6 papers each. The list of the session's acts is a list.
counted_item_by_item.The articles of impeachment against Judg: The finder joins the committee's report of 26 March 1804 and its report of 30 November 1804 into items of 9 and 10 papers. They are two reports, the second made on a new reference and adopted by the House, so each is its own group under the Chase parent, as 1809 kept a Senate bill apart from the act: 6 papers each (the National Intelligencer and the Virginia Argus printed both; together they reach 10 papers).
counted_item_by_item.The papers on General Hamilton's death: The finder joins the documents published after the duel into families of 9 and 10 papers. Counted item by item: the correspondence 9, Hamilton's statement 9, his will 8, Bishop Moore's letter 9, Gouverneur Morris's oration 9; a New York letter of 12 July ('General Hamilton still lives') 5, the order of the funeral procession 5, the Port Folio's obituary 2 (outputs/hamilton_burr_check/README.md checked these on the scans for the talk of 17 November).
counted_item_by_item.The coroner's jury's verdict: The papers report it in three forms: the verdict quoted ('That Aaron Burr, Esq. Vice President of the United States, was guilty of the murder of Alexander Hamilton'; NI, VA, OP, EN, RIR, BJ), a shorter New York Gazette paragraph ('brought in a verdict of MURDER by AARON BURR'; ADA, BJ, EN, JPG, NHG) and the Norfolk Gazette's own words. Counted together as the verdict, as 1805 counted the accounts of Chase's acquittal and 1807 the Burr verdict: 10 papers, 13 printings (the Berkeley and Jefferson Intelligencer printed two accounts, the Enquirer three). The quoted verdict alone is in 6 papers.
counted_item_by_item.General Moreau: The finder joins the Moreau items of the year. Counted by their own words: the letter attributed to him by Les Nouvelles à la Main (No. II) 7, the same newsletter's No. III 7, the London paragraph on his banishment 8, and his letter to the First Consul of 17 Ventose, printed during his trial, 5 (in two translations).
counted_item_by_item.The documents with the message of Novemb: Counted by Document No. I, the extract of Cevallos's letter to Pinckney: 9 papers. Three papers (EN, JPG, KG) also printed the National Intelligencer's paragraph listing the documents ('the message of the president was accompanied by various documents, among which were'), a summary in other words, which is not counted.
counted_item_by_item.The House's daily proceedings: From November 1804 most papers reprinted the House's daily proceedings in the same words, so the finder makes items of 7 to 11 papers out of single paragraphs of those reports (motions, votes, memorials referred). Each paragraph is counted by its own words as an item, as 1806 counted Mr. Gregg's resolution, 1809 Mr. Giles's and 1800 Mr. Livingston's; the day's proceedings as a whole are a digest. One paragraph reaches 9 papers and is admitted: Mr. Griswold's motion of 12 November for an inquiry into drawbacks of duties at New Orleans (the committee's report on it, in 3 more papers, only quotes it). The others are in 8 or fewer: the motion to present a sword to Captain Decatur (8 as moved; the resolution as passed, printed by authority, in 3), the House's vote on it (8), the committee's return from the President on it (8), Mr. Randolph's question on the articles against Judge Chase (7), a memorial of 237 American citizens in Louisiana (7).
counted_item_by_item.Standing notices printed in successive i: The Secretary of State's notice that the amendment has been ratified ran in successive issues of several papers (the National Intelligencer four times, the Virginia Argus, the Rhode-Island Republican and the Kentucky Gazette three times each, the Enquirer twice); each printing counts, as 1807 counted the proclamation calling Congress: 17 printings in 7 papers.
